implementation_notes: The standard library ships the exact value type: scala.concurrent.duration.Deadline (Deadline.now, hasTimeLeft, timeLeft) measured on System.nanoTime, so it is immune to clock changes, plus the duration DSL for 3.seconds.fromNow and for advancing or shortening a deadline. Carry one Deadline through the call chain, check hasTimeLeft before starting a stage, and derive every wait from timeLeft - which is negative once overdue. Futures themselves have no timeout: Await.result(f, deadline.timeLeft) or a timed combinator is how a hop enforces the remainder, while the dominant effect libraries expose fiber-level timeout combinators over the same idea, adding real cancellation that plain Future lacks.
pitfalls: Await.result needs a finite duration; a fresh constant per hop re-creates independent timeouts. Derive from deadline.timeLeft and do not block a thread that the executor itself needs (deadlock risk).
Deadline is measured against System.nanoTime and cannot be serialized meaningfully; send the remaining duration, not the Deadline, across a network hop.
Future has no cancellation: cancelling the waiting side does not stop the computation, so an effect system (fiber cancellation) is required when real cancellation propagation matters.
timeLeft of an overdue deadline is negative; passing it to Await or a timeout combinator can throw or fire immediately, so check hasTimeLeft first.
